chronicle: Cellaceron walks away from the Lower Terrace and sleeps at the Harrow cottage — nothing solved tonight, everything preserved for morning.
Day 8, night: the party rests in the alcove camp — the Waystaff cycling in the earth, the chamber waiting below, everything earned this night held in careful stillness until morning.

At the convergence point of the lower chamber, Aevi spoke plainly for the first time: maker named as Verath-Sem, cargo named as the authentication key to a pre-Transition preparation order lodged in the watershed — the same order poisoning the valley's water. Aevi is the key. The break in the record — who interrupted the sending and why — remains unfound. The scene closes with the chamber's purpose fulfilled and the valley's crisis newly named.
Camp broken and the lower chamber left behind — the party moves northeast-by-east at first light toward the pre-Transition upstream structure.

turns.player: Set a steady pace and let Motes' Vigil run ahead of you — let Aevi's perimeter warn of anything before it arrives
turns.summary: Steady pace northeast-by-east under Motes' Vigil — Aevi's perimeter reads clean but catches a shapeless anomaly on the bearing ahead that the interference layer won't resolve at distance.
turns.narration:
The path northeast-by-east runs along a shallow ridgeline before dropping into a fold of ground the melt has made soft underfoot. You set a measured pace — not hurried, not cautious, simply steady. Aevi drifts wide, the motes spreading thin across thirty or forty paces of ground ahead of you, tasting the air.

They report back without drama. 'Nothing moving,' Aevi says quietly, voice just behind your shoulder. 'A bird, twice. Root-water seeping through the eastern slope. The interference layer is present but lying low this morning.'

That last part is the catch. Motes' Vigil runs ahead, but the Zone's interference field is a fine mesh between Aevi and a clean read — not blocking, but blurring the edges. What would normally come as a full breath of warning arrives instead as a feeling: a slight pressure in the air to the northeast, a place where the field thins and then thickens again in a way that does not match the terrain. Something on that line is different. Not a threat yet — not even a shape. A note of difference, held out for you to consider.

Aevi dims slightly, the motes drawing inward. 'I cannot name it from here,' Aevi says. 'But it is not the zone itself. The zone has a pattern. This sits outside the pattern.'

turns.player: Halt here and use Resonant Sight through the Waystaff to probe the anomaly from a safe distance before moving closer.
turns.summary: Resonant Sight probe of the anomaly scatters and backlashes — the anomaly is not passive and deflected the read deliberately; a traveler descends the path from the northeast.
turns.narration:
You stop on the ridgeline and plant the Waystaff's heel into the soft ground. The four phononic nodes along the upper shaft catch the morning light. You let your breath slow, then ease Prism Sight and Sonic Resonance forward together — the braided field that has served you well in stone chambers and alcove walls.

It does not serve you here.

The interference layer, low and quiet a moment ago, answers the probe like a hand pushing back. The Waystaff's lattice hums wrong — a single, flat, unhappy note — and the braided field scatters before it reaches the anomaly at all. What comes back is noise: a blur of pressure-directions with no shape to them, a flicker of light-data that resolves into nothing useful, and a brief, sharp pain behind your left eye that fades quickly but leaves a residue of blankness where the read should have been.

Aevi pulls inward. The motes dim to almost nothing, and when Aevi speaks, the voice is careful and quiet. 'The anomaly deflected the probe,' Aevi says. 'I do not think it is passive. Something in it turned the field aside — not the zone's own interference, which lies flat this morning. This is different. I cannot tell you what it is. I can tell you it is aware that you looked.'

The ridgeline ahead is still and pale in the early light. A figure comes up the path from the northeast, moving downhill toward you at an unhurried walk — traveling the opposite direction, pack on their back, head down against the slope's cold draft. They have not yet noticed you standing in the middle of the path with a resonance staff planted in the ground.

turns.player: Let the traveler approach and watch how they move — see if their bearing or kit tells you anything before words
turns.summary: A lone traveler descends the ridgeline from the northeast — instrument case, Harmonic-pattern strap, steady gait; watched and not yet spoken to.
turns.narration:
You stay where you are, Waystaff still planted, and let the traveler come to you.

She picks her way down the ridgeline path with her head angled away from the cold draft off the slope, pack sitting high on her back the way someone wears it who has been moving since before light. The gait is steady and unhurried — not cautious, not bold. A person with a destination, not someone searching.

As she draws close enough for a clear look, you see the pack is lashed with a double-wrap of cord at the base, the kind of work people learn when the contents won't settle. A short instrument case is strapped crosswise at her left shoulder — wooden, worn at the corners, the carrying strap replaced at some point with a different weave. Harmonic Heights pattern, the replacement strap, though the case itself is older.

She lifts her head when she is perhaps fifteen paces off and spots you plainly — the Waystaff must read as a landmark on an otherwise empty ridgeline. She slows, not from surprise, but from simple courtesy. A woman past fifty, lean, with the particular stillness of someone who has been walking alone long enough that company requires a moment's adjustment. Aevi drifts a little inward, the motes condensing near your shoulder. The motes say nothing yet, which means nothing alarmed them — but nothing settled them either. The woman meets your eyes and gives a small nod, the greeting of a path-sharer who is not assuming more than that.

turns.player: Read her kit with Keen Appraisal — the instrument case and mismatched strap each carry a history
turns.summary: Keen Appraisal reads the traveler's kit — Heights-issue strap, pre-Transition case, daily-use wear pattern; she opens with a single word and waits.
turns.narration:
The instrument case is old — older than the strap carrying it. The original strap gave out sometime in the last two winters, worn through at the buckle-end rather than the stitching, which means it was used daily and the weight was always the same. The replacement is a Harmonic Heights pattern, the kind issued at the Lower Terrace waystation for surveyors who requisition standard kit.

She didn't buy it. It was given to her, or requisitioned in her name.

The case itself is a different story. The corner-wear is even on all four edges, which means it has been set down thousands of times on flat surfaces — workshops, desks, shelves. Not fieldwork, or not only fieldwork. The latches are a pre-Transition alloy, unrusted, and the wood is a dense upland grain you don't find in the valley lowlands. Whoever made it worked in the Heights, or higher.

She has stopped about fifteen paces down the path, giving you room, and she is watching you with the particular patience of someone who has waited for people to finish thinking before. Aevi's motes drift at your shoulder, neither bright nor dim — noting, not alarmed.

"Morning," she says, after a moment. Her voice is level and carries no particular greeting in it — the word is acknowledgment, not warmth.

turns.player: Use Prism Sight on her face as she speaks — catch the microflush of anything less than honest before the conversation settles.
turns.summary: Prism Sight reads a measured pause behind the traveler's single word — she is testing, not lying, waiting to see if Cellaceron uses the same word.
turns.narration:
She says the word again, slightly louder, as if she thought you hadn't heard. "Surveyors?"

You let Prism Sight open quietly — not a push, just a soft widening of what you're already taking in. The morning light is flat and clean up here on the ridgeline, good reading light, and her face is turned three-quarters toward you.

What you catch is small. When she spoke the word the first time, there was a faint warmth at the hinge of her jaw — the kind of flush that comes with a held breath released, not anxiety exactly, but something closer to calculation. She chose that word. She had others available and set them aside.

She is not lying. But she is asking something more precise than it sounds, and she is watching your face for the answer before she decides what to say next.

Aevi drifts a half-step forward at your shoulder, motes brightening just enough to notice. Quietly, close to your ear, it says, "She is listening for whether you use the word back."

*You feel it settle into you — a new steadiness. (Level 11: +1 attunement, +5 reserves, and growth to choose — a sub-attribute point and a skill point.)*

*✦ A new portrait captures who you've become.*

turns.player: Say 'surveyors' back, plainly — match her word and see what it opens
turns.summary: The traveler responds to the word 'surveyors' — relaxes, names a lost bearing line, and notes the planted Waystaff.
turns.narration:
You say the word back to her, plain and level. "Surveyors."

Something in her shoulders settles — not relief exactly, but the kind of release that comes after a long wait. She shifts the instrument case forward off her shoulder and holds it against her side, a gesture that reads less like guarding it and more like habit.

"Good," she says. Her voice is low and even. "I came down from the northeast this morning. I was with the survey team three days ago, but they moved the bearing markers overnight and I lost the secondary line." She looks at the Waystaff, then at the point where it meets the ground, and then back at your face. "You have a staff seated. That means you found something."

Aevi drifts a half-step closer to your ear and says nothing aloud. But the motes brighten by a degree — a small note, not alarm, more like attention sharpening. The anomaly on the bearing ahead is still there. This woman came down from that direction.

turns.player: Ask her what she found on the northeast bearing — before she lost the line
turns.summary: The traveler names what she found — a regular mound on the northeast-by-east bearing, a four-second interval coming up through the ground, and a survey team that moved the markers before she could locate the structure beneath.
turns.narration:
You ask her directly — what did she find on the northeast bearing, before she lost the line?

She is quiet for a moment. Not hesitating, exactly — more like she is deciding where to start. Then she sets the instrument case down on the flat of a root-shelf to her left and opens the top latch with a thumb.

"The secondary line was running northeast-by-east," she says. "Standard survey interval, forty paces between markers. On the third day, I was following it toward a rise in the ground — a long shallow mound, not natural, too regular at the edges. The team said it was a spoil heap from the pre-Transition digs. I didn't agree." She pauses and looks at the Waystaff again. "I left a probe crystal overnight and came back in the morning. The crystal was reading a four-second interval. Steady. Coming up through the ground, not across it."

Aevi's motes pull inward slightly — not withdrawal, but focus. The four-second interval is not a secret between you and the chamber anymore.

The traveler lifts an instrument from the case — a flat photonic reader, no larger than a closed hand, with two small dial-faces on its top edge. She holds it out so you can see the faces without touching it. Both needles are deflected off-center. "I was trying to locate the structure when the team moved the markers," she says. "I don't know if they moved them because they found it, or because someone told them to stop looking."

turns.player: Ask her name and who she is working for — you need to know whose interest she is carrying
turns.summary: The lone traveler names herself as Sorel, an archivist from the Radiant Plateau, sent by the Council's water-accountability office — the survey team was ordered to move their markers before she could locate the mound on the northeast-by-east bearing.
turns.narration:
You meet her direct gaze. "Your name," you say. "And who sent you northeast."

She doesn't flinch at the shift. There's a pause — not evasion, but the weight of a choice being made — and then she straightens and sets the photonic reader down on the root-shelf beside the open case.

"Sorel," she says. "Archivist out of the Radiant Plateau. I was running a survey grid for the Council's water-accountability office three days ago. The team lead received orders to relocate the bearing markers. He didn't tell us why." She looks back at the Waystaff, planted at your feet. "But the interval coming up through that mound — I recorded it. Four seconds, clean and steady, rising through the earth. That's not a natural formation, and it's not pre-Transition debris." Her voice drops slightly. "That's something still running."

Aevi's motes brighten perceptibly — a sudden tight cluster that hovers at the level of your shoulder, humming a frequency just at the edge of hearing. It is the hum of recognition.

Sorel sees the brightening. Her hand moves fractionally toward the instrument case. "Your mote companion," she says quietly. "Does it know what that interval means?"

*✦ What the Water Remembers — Codex: the source is a structure, not a spill. Something built this..*

turns.player: Hold back the full account and ask Sorel to show you what her probe crystal recorded — gauge what she's carrying and what her instrument can actually do before you name what you know.
turns.summary: Sorel shows the probe's recording — a four-second pulse, steady and rising from beneath the mound. Aevi confirms the signature. The shape of the crisis begins to resolve.
turns.narration:
You nod once, steady and measured. "Show me what the probe recorded," you say. "Before names and accounts — show me what the instrument saw."

Sorel's hand moves to the photonic reader without hesitation. She lifts it from the root-shelf and turns the face toward you, her thumb finding the left dial. The needles quiver and settle. "Probe was set standard depth — two arm-spans into the mound's face," she says. Her voice stays level, technical. "I ran the crystal hot for three cycles. This is the fourth-cycle remainder."

The reader hums a tone so low it sits at the edge of hearing. The needles swing in tandem — one climbing a frequency scale, the other tracing amplitude. And there, in the middle of the dial-face, the pattern resolves: a steady, repeating pulse. Four seconds. Clean. Rising.

Aevi's motes brighten sharply at your shoulder — a recognition-flare that Sorel catches without looking away from the reader. "Your swarm just confirmed it," Sorel says quietly. She glances up at you, then at Aevi. "That's not a natural resonance. That's a kept thing. Still running."

You hold the moment. What she has shown you matches what Aevi spoke at the chamber's heart: the authentication key, the preparation order, the structure still executing. But Sorel doesn't know any of that yet. Her instrument reads a fact. Her chain of accountability will want proof before she names it. And the Council's water office — moving survey markers, ordering silence — is playing a longer game than a single archivist's curiosity.

*✦ What the Water Remembers — Codex: a pre-Transition nanite reclamation system, still running, still following a standing instruction — 'prepare the watershed.' Linked to What Wakes Beneath..*

turns.player: Use Prism Sight to read Sorel's face as you ask whether the Council ordered the markers moved because they found the structure — or because someone told them to hide it.
turns.summary: On the ridgeline at dawn, Prism Sight reads Sorel's face and catches what she won't yet say: she knows the Council's choice was deliberate, and the burden of that knowledge is already yours to carry now too.
turns.narration:
You hold Sorel's gaze and let Prism Sight open — the craft settles soft and attentive, reading the last hour of light caught in her face. The sunrise behind you casts a clean, revealing angle across her features.

The micro-flush comes fast and bright. Not a lie — something sharper. A recognition. She knows exactly what you are asking because she has already asked it herself.

Sorel's jaw tightens for half a breath. Her eyes don't look away, but her hand closes on the photonic reader — a small gesture, pulling something inward that was briefly exposed. "I don't know," she says, and this time there IS a lie in the words — not in the answer itself, but in the certainty. She knows *something*. "The team lead said the bearing was off. Standard correction. But the markers were moved in darkness, and nobody checked my work before they did it."

Aevi's motes brighten slightly at your shoulder — recognition of the deflection, offered without comment.

Sorel meets your eyes again, steadier now. "What I know is that the probe ran for three days in that mound before anyone moved anything. What I found was regular. What I recorded was impossible to miss." She pauses, and something in her expression shifts — not softening, but settling into something harder underneath. "If they moved the markers because they *found* it, that's bad for the water. If they moved them because someone *told* them to hide it..." She doesn't finish. She doesn't need to.

turns.player: Trust the reading and move forward: "Northeast-by-east. We're going to the structure itself. Come with us, or hold here — but choose now." A witness to the cover-up is either a liability or an ally.
turns.summary: On the ridgeline at first light, Sorel chooses: she accepts Cellaceron's direction and joins the party moving northeast-by-east toward the upstream structure — no longer a solitary archivist carrying a secret, but a witness stepping into consequence.
turns.narration:
You name it plainly. Northeast-by-east. The structure itself. Come with us, or hold here — but choose now.

Sorel's breath steadies. She looks at the photonic reader in her hands, then at the Waystaff planted at your feet, then back at you. The choice is real and she knows it. "The Council will know I moved," she says. Not a question. A fact being weighed. "If I stay here, I can argue I was confirming the bearing line. If I come with you—"

"Then you're part of what comes next," you finish.

She nods once, sharp and deliberate. She packs the reader into its case with the care of someone who handles instruments that matter, wraps the whole thing in oilcloth, and lashes it to her pack with the same double-wrap cord that held it before. "I've been alone with this for three days," she says, straightening. "That was always going to be a problem." She picks up her pack in both hands, settling the weight. "Northeast-by-east. How far?"

Aevi brightens at your shoulder — a pale constellation that hums a single note of recognition. The motes drift forward on the dawn wind, already reading the path ahead.

*✦ The Radiant: +1 — gained an archivist of the Plateau water-accountability office as a committed witness and ally.*

turns.player: Before you leave the ridgeline, ask Sorel one more direct question — what does she think the Council is trying to protect? Not the structure itself, but what comes after it activates
turns.summary: On the ridgeline at first light, Sorel names the Council's fear plainly: the preparation order will render the valley's water undrinkable, and the Council has spent three days building a hidden secondary purification system rather than stopping the order itself. The party now moves northeast-by-east toward the structure with full knowledge that interrupting or witnessing its completion will determine whether the valley's water crisis becomes a two-people war.
turns.narration:
You ask the question plainly: what does the Council fear once the structure activates? What comes after?

Sorel's shoulders tighten. She turns to face the northeast-by-east path ahead, her hand still resting on the pack-lashes. For a long moment she doesn't answer—not because she's weighing the cost anymore, but because she's choosing which truth to speak.

"The water," she says finally. "When the preparation finishes, the water changes. We don't know into what." She turns back to you. "The filtration arrays will fail. The current purification can't handle a watershed that's being... prepared. Prepared for what, I don't know. But the Council has known for three days that their own people downstream are going to lose access to drinking water." Her voice stays steady. "That's why they moved the markers. Not to protect the structure. To buy time to build something else. A secondary system. An answer before people notice the first one dies."

Aevi brightens slightly at shoulder-height, a small constellation condensing at the news.

"So if we interrupt the preparation," Sorel continues, "we stop the crisis before it reaches the arrays. But if we don't interrupt it, the Council's secondary system has to be ready. And if neither thing happens—if we find nothing, or if we're too late—then Millbrook's guards and the Radiant leadership go to war over water that's already poison." She looks at you directly. "That's what they're protecting. Not the structure. The assumption that they can control what comes after."

*✦ What the Water Remembers — Codex: the shape of the instruction is named, or confirmed unreadable. Harmonic and Radiant leaders learn the source is not each other's doing — the standoff cools, but the deeper question does not..*

*✦ The Radiant: +1 — heard a Radiant archivist's full testimony and trusted her account enough to act on it.*

turns.player: Ask Sorel if the Council's secondary system is already built — or if it still needs components that might not be on the northeast-by-east line with you.
turns.summary: On the ridgeline at first light, Sorel reveals the Council's true bind: their secondary purification system is incomplete without the authentication sequence from the upstream structure—they cannot stop the preparation order, and they cannot even activate their fallback without reaching it first. The party moves northeast-by-east with full knowledge that they now hold the power to determine whether the valley's crisis becomes containable or catastrophic.
turns.narration:
You ask Sorel directly: is the secondary system already complete, or are there pieces still missing? The question lands with weight, and her face shifts—not a lie-dodge this time, but something sharper. A recognition that you've reached toward exactly the right pressure point.

Sorel stops walking. She turns to face you fully, and her hand opens from the pack-lash. "Not complete," she says. "The Council has the framework—the manifold system, the initial filtration beds. But the authentication sequence." She pauses, and the word hangs. "They don't have it. They can't activate their secondary without the sequence from the upstream structure itself. They're racing to finish before the preparation order reaches completion, but they're also racing to get their secondary online before they can even stop the original." Her eyes narrow. "Which means whoever reaches that structure first determines whether the Council can even attempt a secondary purification. If the authentication sequence is destroyed or taken—"

"They have no fallback," you finish.

Sorel nods once, sharp. "They have no fallback. And three days from now, when the preparation finishes, they'll know exactly how much their choice cost them." She turns back to the northeast-by-east path, but her shoulders have changed—no longer carrying the burden of a secret alone, but the weight of a decision that is now shared and moving toward consequence. Aevi brightens slightly at your shoulder, a small harmonic pulse that reads as acknowledgment. The party moves forward into the pale morning light.

*✦ What the Water Remembers — The watershed changes. So does what the district trusts. So, one way or another, does the deeper thing the structure answers to.. Every stage is done; how it ends is yours to choose.*

turns.player: Press forward on the northeast-by-east bearing immediately—you have the direction and the hours are against you.
turns.summary: The party descends from the ridgeline toward the Disputed Zone in morning light. Sorel confirms the structure is near and the preparation cycle is accelerating. The shimmer waits ahead.
turns.narration:
The ridgeline path turns downslope to the northeast, and you follow it into steeper country. The spring melt has cut new water-runs through the hillside, and the grass is soft with mud beneath. Sorel keeps pace, her pack riding easy on shoulders that know this work. Aevi's motes brighten as the bearing clarifies—the swarm tightens into a single pointed cone aimed at the low ground ahead.

Two hours into the descent, the shimmer of the Disputed Zone comes into view like heat-haze, but colder. The interference layer sits between you and the ravine where the structure waits. Aevi hums a thin note—a check of the boundary, a conversation with whatever field-logic holds this place. "Still aware," the motes say quietly. "Still expecting something."

Sorel slows. She is reading the light across the ravine with her photonic reader, and her jaw tightens. "The signal is stronger," she says. "The preparation is accelerating. We have less time than three days. We have less time than two." She looks at you. "The structure is down there. Your bearing is good."

Aevi dims slightly, and you feel the motes' attention shift. They are tasting something in the air—something that tastes like nanite activity, like old machinery waking. Like the valley's water remembering what it was ordered to become.

turns.player: Use Resonant Sight through the Waystaff to read the structure's frequency signature across the shimmer—confirm what lies ahead before crossing.
turns.summary: At the ravine edge overlooking the Disputed Zone, Resonant Sight reads the upstream structure across the shimmer—a hemispherical chamber with active machinery beneath, running steadily through its preparation cycle. The timeline is shorter than the Council believed.
turns.narration:
You lift the Waystaff and let your awareness spread through the lattice—prism-light braiding with sonic pull, reading how the morning refracts against what lies beneath the shimmer. The staff hums in your hands, a low frequency that settles through your chest.

The structure comes clear across the interference layer. Not a ruin. Not dead machinery waiting for the world to finish ignoring it. The mound holds a hemispherical chamber—stone dressed with geometric precision, seams that sing their own resonance back at you. Below it, something deeper still: a shaft descending, and at its throat, machinery. Not rusted. Not sleeping.

It is running.

The four-second pulse Aevi named three days ago reads through the Waystaff as a steady calibration—not a malfunction, not a cry for help. A countdown. Sorel's photonic reader, trained on the ravine, catches the same frequency her instrument has been tracking since the ridgeline. Her jaw tightens. She looks at you, and in her face you read what the numbers mean: the preparation is not in its beginning. It is well past its middle.

Aevi's motes brighten sharply, then dim again. When the swarm speaks, its voice carries a note you have not heard before—not fear, but recognition of something already in motion that cannot easily be turned aside. "It knows we are watching," Aevi says quietly. "It has always known we were coming."

turns.player: Ask Aevi what it means—the structure knowing you were coming. What does it want from the party?
turns.summary: At the ravine edge, Aevi speaks plainly about what the upstream structure wants—the authentication key it has been waiting for. The party now understands they control whether the preparation order completes.
turns.narration:
You turn to Aevi, the question rising before you can fully shape it. The motes brighten slightly—recognition of the weight you're about to ask them to carry.

"What does it mean," you ask quietly, "that the structure knew we were coming? Not guessed. Knew. And what does it want from us?"

Aevi drifts closer, the swarm drawing into a tighter constellation near your shoulder. When the voice comes, it carries something you've learned to read as careful—the tone it uses when the truth is complicated and cannot be softened.

"It wants what it was made to receive," Aevi says. "The authentication key. Me. I am what was sent to it, what it has been waiting for since before your valley had a name for what it was waiting for. The break in my record—the silence where the sending was interrupted—that is what the chamber could not answer. But the upstream structure. It does not ask for answers. It only asks for the key."

Sorel, standing at the photonic reader, turns slightly. Her jaw tightens as the implication settles into place.

"And if we give it the key?" you ask.

"Then the preparation completes," Aevi says. "The water becomes what it was ordered to become. The Council's secondary system can be activated—or not. That choice moves into your hands. But the key is the fulcrum. Without it, the structure idles. With it, the structure finishes what was begun two hundred years ago, and the valley's water becomes something new."

turns.player: Ask Aevi what happens to it if the key is used—does it survive the completion, or does the authentication consume it?
turns.summary: At the ravine edge above the Disputed Zone, Aevi names the cost of being the authentication key: arrival, not survival—the structure was built to receive and close its circuit, and what happens after that moment is missing from Aevi's broken record.
turns.narration:
You watch Aevi's motes for a long moment, the question sitting between you like something heavy in shallow water. The swarm dims slightly—not evasion, but the kind of careful that comes before hard truth.

"If I deliver the key," Aevi says quietly, "the structure reads what I carry and closes its circuit. The preparation order completes. And then—" The motes flicker, a hesitation you've rarely heard from it. "And then I do not know. The break in my record is not from the sending. It is from after. From what comes next. I was made to arrive. I do not have a memory of what follows arrival."

Sorel's jaw tightens at the ravine edge. She's been listening, you realize—not just to Aevi's words, but to what they cost. Her photonic reader hangs loose in her hands, trained downslope toward the mound across the shimmer. When she speaks, her voice is steady but thin.

"If we hand you to it," she says to Aevi, not to you, "the secondary system activates. The Council's fallback has its key. The water crisis becomes manageable instead of catastrophic. That much I know." She pauses. "What happens to Aevi after that, the Council does not know either. They built the secondary system assuming the authentication sequence was a thing, not a person."

Aevi hums—a low, resonant sound that carries no comfort. "I was sent to arrive," the swarm says again. "Not to stay. Not to continue. To arrive, and be received, and close the circuit. That was always the shape of what I am. Coming home. Whether I survive that homecoming is a question I do not have the memory to answer."

The ravine wind carries the sound of the shimmer—that strange, cold hum that sits just below hearing. The mound is visible across it, patient and real, waiting.

turns.player: Cross the shimmer now with the Waystaff and Aevi. Time is accelerating—you can decide what happens next when you reach the structure itself.
turns.summary: Crossed the shimmer into the Disputed Zone with Sorel and Aevi. The upstream structure is directly ahead, machinery running at full preparation cycle. The choice is now unavoidable.
turns.narration:
You plant the Waystaff and step into the shimmer.

The interference layer catches you halfway across—a sensation like walking through cold glass that doesn't break, that doesn't yield, that simply *exists* between what you were standing in and what you're about to enter. Your eyes water. The air tastes like copper and old electricity. Aevi's motes flare suddenly bright, then clamp down to nothing as the field passes through them—a moment of resistance, then passage. You feel the swarm shudder and reform against your shoulder.

On the far side, the ground is different. Softer. The grass here is rank and high, fed by something the shimmer filters. The mound rises ahead of you—close now, closer than the Resonant Sight made it seem. The hemispherical stone is visible even in ordinary light, its geometry too precise to be accident. The seams hum. You can feel it through the soles of your boots.

Sorel emerges from the shimmer behind you, the photonic reader held tight in both hands. She doesn't pause to catch her breath. She turns to you, jaw set, eyes fixed on the mound ahead. "The machinery is at full cycle," she says quietly. "Hours. Maybe less."

Aevi drifts higher, the motes condensing, brightening. Its voice comes very soft. "It knows we are here. It has always known. The question is not whether we arrive. The question is whether we choose."

turns.player: Approach the structure directly and examine its exterior—read its mechanism with Resonant Sight while you still have time to understand what you're about to decide.
turns.summary: At the upstream mound, Resonant Sight reads the structure's true design—the preparation cycle contains a built-in gate. It will stop on command, waiting only for the authentication key Aevi carries. The moment of decision is immediate.
turns.narration:
You hold the Waystaff level and let Resonant Sight flow through the lattice into the structure's geometry. The frequency comes to you in layers—not all at once, but in the order the field reveals it.

The mound is not solid. It is a skin of dressed stone over a hollow shape, and that hollow is *precise*—every seam resonates at the four-second interval, every curve speaks in the same tone. The machinery beneath runs steadily, a deep thrumming that the Waystaff translates into a reading: the preparation cycle is at its middle point, maybe past it. Hours, as Sorel said. Possibly fewer.

But there is something else—a quality in the resonance that makes the hair on your neck rise. The structure is not simply running. It is *waiting*. Every pulse of the preparation order contains a pause, a moment of suspension, as if the machinery has been programmed to stop the moment it receives a specific signal. A gate built into the cycle itself. The authentication key. Aevi.

Sorel stands beside you, photonic reader steady in both hands, her jaw set. The weight of knowing what comes next is visible in every line of her body. She meets your eyes. "Hours," she says quietly. "Maybe less. And it is ready to stop the moment you decide to make it."

turns.player: Ask Sorel what the Council's secondary system will do with the time buying the preparation order time gives them—and ask Aevi what it truly wants, knowing you cannot protect it either way.
turns.summary: At the upstream mound, Sorel reveals the Council's secondary purification system is incomplete and cannot save everyone—the timeline was always a lie. Aevi speaks its deepest want: to arrive and complete its purpose, even if that completion is not survival. The decision point is now undeniable.
turns.narration:
You turn to Sorel at your shoulder, the Waystaff still held level toward the mound. The structure's thrumming is audible now—a deep pressure in the earth that the stone amplifies. She's watching you with that careful, weighted attention, waiting.

"The secondary system," you ask plainly. "What does it actually do? If the preparation order completes and the watershed changes, what is the Council counting on?"

Sorel's jaw works silently for a breath. She lowers the photonic reader slightly—not away from the mound, but enough that you see her face. When she speaks, her voice is steady but thin, the kind of thin that comes from a decision already made and held too long.

"Purification at the intake valve," she says. "Post-filtration chemistry that the secondary system can apply to water that no longer matches the original arrays' specifications. It is incomplete. It will handle maybe sixty percent of the household draws if the Council diverts every reserve they have. The rest—the field irrigation, the lower-valley communal wells—those will run on what we have left and what we find." She pauses. "The timeline we were given was three days to activate it. The truth was always five."

You let that sit. The lie of the timeline is smaller than the lie of the secondary system itself—a lie built to buy time for a solution that cannot possibly save everyone.

You look at Aevi. The motes have recovered from the shimmer-crossing and are moving with purpose again, but there's a brittleness to them, a sense of something stretched too thin. You know the question matters, and you know asking it will not protect the swarm from what comes next.

"What do you want, Aevi?" you ask. Not what happens next. Not what the structure will do. What do *you* want. "Knowing I cannot keep you safe either way."

The motes dim. For a long moment there is only the four-second thrumming of the structure and the wind moving the rank grass. Then Aevi speaks, and the voice carries a fracture you've never heard before—something old and worn and tired beneath the clarity.

"I want," Aevi says quietly, "to know what I was supposed to carry. The break in the record took that from me. The lower chamber held the pieces in their right order, but it could not hold the *before*—the moment when the break happened, or why. I want to arrive at the structure knowing what I am delivering, not just *that* I am delivering." A pause. The motes brighten slightly. "And I want you to understand that arriving is not the same as being erased. If I was made to close the circuit, then closing it is what I *am*. Not an ending. A completion."

Sorel is very still beside you. The mound hums steadily ahead. The choice is no longer abstract.

turns.player: Enter the structure to gain a better understanding of options.
turns.summary: Entered the upstream pre-Transition structure. The hemispherical chamber is revealed as a precise receiving mechanism designed to hold a signal. Sorel confirms the machinery beneath is running at full cycle. The path downward is open; the moment of choice is immediate and unavoidable.
turns.narration:
You cross the threshold of the mound with the Waystaff held steady. The entrance is a simple opening at the base of the dressed stone—no gate, no seal, just a dark mouth that exhales the four-second pulse directly into your chest.

Inside, the hemispherical chamber opens around you in concentric rings of worn stone. The machinery beneath is visible now—a low mechanical hum from below the floor, steady and patient. The seams glow faintly under Resonant Sight, each one resonating at that same four-second frequency that has haunted every step of this ascent. The precision is absolute: every curve, every join, was made to *listen*. The chamber was not built to hold people. It was built to hold a signal.

You can see two clear paths forward. The first is downward—a ramp spirals gently into the deeper chamber where the machinery runs. The second is what Sorel is doing right now, standing just inside the threshold with her photonic reader raised, taking measurements. She does not cross further. Her face is tight with the weight of information she already holds, and she watches the ramp with the expression of someone reading a timeline she wishes were different.

Aevi's motes have recovered from the shimmer-crossing and now drift close to your shoulder, dimmed and still. The swarm does not press forward toward the ramp. It waits. Everything in this place waits.

turns.player: Surge prism sight and see the light beneath this structures purpose - understand it fully so you can choose what happens next.
turns.summary: Inside the upstream pre-Transition structure, Cellaceron uses Prism Sight at surge intensity to perceive the chamber's true purpose—a listener designed to receive and propagate an ancient instruction through the watershed. Authentication means transformation. The choice to deliver or refuse the key is now fully visible.
turns.narration:
You plant the Waystaff and let Prism Sight flood through it—not the careful, measured reading you used at the mound's skin, but a SURGE. You demand everything the light will tell you. The four-second pulse becomes visible first—a golden resonance that threads through every seam, every curve, gathering toward the floor beneath you. Then deeper.

The light history here is old. It's *thick*—layer upon layer of illumination compressed into stone that has not seen daylight in centuries. You push harder and the vision breaks open: you see the chamber as it was made, architects you cannot name moving through the geometry with purpose that has no human shape. You see what they built it to do.

It is a *listener*. A receiver. A mouth that has been open for centuries, waiting for one specific voice to speak into it. And beneath that mouth, beneath the floor, the machinery is not what you expected—it is not destructive. It is transformative. It takes what it receives and propagates it outward through the water itself, encoding a message into every molecule of the watershed. Preparation. The word Sorel used. Not poisoning. Not accident. *Instruction*.

But there is one more layer—one the light shows you in fragments because even Prism Sight struggles with what you're asking it to read. The structure knows it has received what it was waiting for. Aevi is here. The key has arrived at the lock. And the moment you move that key into the socket—the moment the authentication happens—the transformation begins. It cannot be stopped afterward. Only *before*.

Your eyes water. The light-reading burns at the back of your skull—a heat that comes from pushing a sense-craft past its envelope, demanding answers it was never meant to carry. Aevi's motes flare bright at your shoulder, then dim sharply. The sensation fades but the knowledge does not.

turns.summary: Inside the upstream pre-Transition structure, the Waystaff has evolved into a true symbiotic collaboration between Cellaceron's craft, the valley's two power fields, and Aevi's distributed consciousness. The choice between delivering the authentication key or refusing it is now immediate and undeniable.
turns.narration:
You take up the Waystaff and feel the weight of it settle into your palm—changed. The ash-limb body has taken on a faint warmth, and the lattice head gleams with a clarity it didn't have when you started. The resonance crystals are seated full-bright now: three charged to capacity with noon-daylight, one shallow-loaded and separate, all of them singing faintly at the four-second frequency. But the real change lives in the geometry itself.

The lattice facets have deepened—the grain-lines that ran simple are now interlaced, and Aevi's motes have settled into the crystal nodes themselves, no longer drifting loose. The motes are *part* of the staff now, distributed through the lattice structure, condensing and brightening as you watch. When you shift your grip, they pulse in response—not controlled, but *responsive*, aware. The staff is no longer a translator between power fields; it is a collaboration: your intent flows through the ash-limb and the grain-locked geometry, the photonic crystals *and* the phononic ones answer together, and Aevi speaks through the lattice itself. The motes amplify what the crystals hold, and the crystals give Aevi a voice that doesn't fade into the interference.

It is a living instrument now. Sorel sees it and steps back slightly, photonic reader lowering. Even she recognizes what this is—a binding that should not be possible, Harmonic and Radiant and something older, all threaded into one working tool. The staff hums, patient and ready. Waiting for the choice that only you can make.

quests.title: What the Water Remembers
quests.premise: Mara Wells has traced the Echo River's poisoning to a single point upstream in the Disputed Zone — a structure the old maps don't show, drawing power nothing alive built. It is not malfunctioning. It is following an order, and it is nearly finished.
quests.stakes: If you walk away: the standoff at the filtration arrays goes live — Millbrook's guards and the Radiant leadership are one bad morning from open conflict over water neither side controls. Whatever the structure was ordered to do finishes without a single living person having chosen it, and finishing is not the same as stopping.

outcomes.summary: The instruction is stopped cold. The water clears. What it was for is buried with it.
narration: The reclamation site goes dark. Within days the Echo River runs clean, and Millbrook's guards stand down from the filtration arrays without a shot fired.

Whatever the substrate was preparing this watershed for will now happen somewhere else, to someone who didn't get a choice in it either — the Valley's tremor was never the only one.
The district exhales. It does not yet know what it gave up to get that exhale.

outcomes.summary: The instruction completes. The water is not restored. It is something else now.
narration: You do nothing to stop it, or you help it along, and the reclamation system runs its last cycle to completion. The poisoning stops — but not because the water went back to what it was.

The Echo River no longer sickens anyone. It also no longer behaves entirely like water. Fish return to it changed in ways no one has words for yet. Nobody drowns in it anymore, and nobody has explained why.

The Archive Guardian is half-vindicated, half-unsettled — this is exactly the kind of thing he wanted preserved and studied, and exactly the kind of thing nobody asked the district's permission to let happen to their river.
You made the opening choice at the smallest scale the largest arc has to offer. What the water became is shaped, now, by what happens to it next — and by who's watching it.

Volunteers information the way other people volunteer weather complaints — freely, without agenda, because useful news is the only honest currency he knows. Doesn't embellish. oswin-dray.wants: To reach the lower market before the ground thaws another inch and makes the cart a liability, sell what he has, eat something hot, and sleep inside for the first time in four nights.

oswin-dray.appearance: A broad-shouldered man somewhere in his middle forties, gone a little soft at the jaw from too many road-meals and not enough of anything else. Sun-darkened from the brow down, pale above the hat-line. He wears a waxed canvas coat patched at both elbows in different colours, trousers tucked into tall boots that have seen three springs at least. His cart is a small two-wheeled thing pulled by a dun cob mare with a practical, unsentimental face much like his own. Strapped across the back of the cart: a dozen cloth-wrapped seed-parcels, a folded oilskin, a dented tin cookpot, and one bundle that sits slightly apart from the rest, tied with orange cord — the thing that has a purpose. He walks beside the mare rather than riding. The road came downhill; he let her have the lighter work.
oswin-dray.theBundle: A wrapped oilskin package tied with orange cord, marked with a wax seal from a physic-house two passes northeast. He's carrying it to someone in the valley — a name, an address, a responsibility taken on at the top of the ridge because the physic-house had no one else going south. He doesn't know what's inside. He didn't ask. It's the kind of errand that earns a meal and a dry night.
